video.title: Watch Me Build an App With AI and Make a Sale in 85 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner builds and markets Only Waivers, a subscription app for creating digital liability waivers and collecting signatures for youth activities. He uses AI coding and advertising tools, runs paid and organic tests, and works through payment and product bugs on camera. He reports one paying customer, but says his advertising spend so far is much higher than the first year’s $13 subscription revenue. The main takeaway is to test demand while building, then use customer behavior and real checkout results to guide fixes and marketing.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; builds and markets the app on camera.

ideas.name: Only Waivers
ideas.one_liner: A self-service app for event organizers to create digital waivers and collect signatures from participants or their parents.
ideas.business_model: Annual subscription or one-off lifetime payment.
ideas.customer: Initially, Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints ward and stake leaders organizing youth activities; also considered gyms, trampoline parks, and tour operators. Parents or guardians sign as end users.
ideas.problem: Paper or PDF permission forms are cumbersome to distribute, print, sign, and collect. Forms can be lost, and organizers may let a child attend without a waiver rather than turn them away.
ideas.offer: An organizer creates an event, optionally uploads a waiver PDF to emulate, and generates a shareable signing link. Signers enter participant and medical information and sign on a phone without creating an account. The organizer can access signed copies in an admin account; the app can provide a generic waiver template.

pricing.notes: The prompt initially specified $13 per year and no free plan. Chris later selected $17 lifetime access, after briefly considering $15 or $20. The first reported external customer bought the yearly plan.

acquisition_channels.details: Created Meta/Facebook ads with an on-camera video aimed at LDS organizers. Started with broad US targeting, then narrowed delivery to Utah after seeing ads served across many states. Used a Meta pixel and UTM parameters to measure activity and compare ads.

acquisition_channels.details: Added a resources page and an SEO-friendly blog about sending liability waivers, with the aim of attracting search traffic and being recommended by ChatGPT.
Planned referral links in confirmation emails and signed-waiver emails so organizers and signers could discover the product.

quote.text: Referral footer in every signed waiver email a lifetime value past year one.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The organizer creates an event and signing link in the web app. Participants or parents complete the form and sign on a phone; signed digital copies are stored for the organizer. The software sends transactional emails. Chris built and maintained the app himself with an AI coding tool, fixed bugs, and handled early customer support. No human service is required for each waiver, though organizers must choose appropriate waiver language and review the records.
unit_economics_claims: The first reported external customer paid for the $13 yearly plan.
Chris said he had spent around $100 on ads and had spent six hours building the app offline by the time of the sale.
He reported a $0.68 Stripe fee on the first external subscription payment.
He said a $200 daily advertising budget could produce roughly 1 to 200 landing page views per day, and estimated that about 15 sales per day would be needed to break even on ad spend.
ideas.startup_cost: Chris paid $12 for the domain. He did not state a full startup cost. He later described roughly $100 of ad spend and six hours of offline app-building work.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: A paying customer bought the yearly plan during the video. The transcript does not state the exact elapsed time from starting the build to that sale.

acquisition.how: Agents can help configure and optimize paid ads, write copy, and support SEO content. A person still needs to choose the audience and offer, make or approve creative, check results, and comply with platform and UK marketing rules.

onboarding.how: Organizers can self-serve event creation and payment, and signers do not need an account. Human review may still be needed when an organizer needs help choosing a template or setting up an event.

delivery.how: The app generates links, collects form data and signatures, and stores copies automatically. Organizers still need to decide whether the waiver suits their event and check that the data is complete.

billing.how: Stripe handles checkout and recurring yearly billing. The founder had to connect the live account and troubleshoot sandbox-mode and checkout issues.

support.how: A contact form can route messages, but early bugs, billing problems, and questions about waiver wording are likely to need founder attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The web app, paid advertising, search, and digital signatures can be used in the UK, but the waiver wording, consumer terms, privacy handling, and treatment of children's sensitive medical information need UK-specific review. The initial LDS positioning and US ad targeting also need adaptation.

risks: A digital signature and template do not by themselves establish that a waiver is suitable or enforceable for a particular organization or activity.
Medical details and children's data create privacy and security obligations; the transcript does not describe a compliance review.
The app initially launched with missing fields and encountered checkout, Stripe live-mode, and contact-form bugs.
A low annual price may not support costly paid acquisition. Chris explicitly reported spending more on ads than the first customer's annual payment.
Paid advertising aimed broadly at cheap clicks may produce traffic from poor-fit audiences; Chris changed targeting after seeing delivery across many states.
A narrow religious niche may limit the initial market, while expansion into gyms, tours, or other organizations may require different forms, branding, and sales processes.
Only one external customer is reported, so retention, repeat usage, referrals, and viable acquisition costs are unproven.
Using a church waiver form as a blueprint requires care; Chris noted that the source form was copyrighted and said not to ship a clone.

tactics.name: Test the offer while the product is being built
steps: Build a minimal version of the product around a problem the founder experiences directly.
Set up an ad campaign before the app is complete so demand can be tested while implementation continues.
Pause ads if checkout is broken so traffic does not continue spending without a path to purchase.
Return to the ad campaign after payment and signup flows work.

quote.text: I'm going to start seeing if I can make ads for this before it's even done because what do I always say? Sell it before you have it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Start with the audience closest to the problem
steps: Begin with the customer group whose problem the founder understands personally.
Write creative using language and examples that group recognizes.
Expand to adjacent customer types only after learning from the first audience.

quote.text: I want to start with the audience that's closest in line with the problem that I'm experience and trying to solve with this product.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use specific creative to qualify paid traffic
steps: Record a short video describing the exact customer, situation, and pain point.
Put niche-specific details in the spoken creative so poor-fit viewers can skip the ad.
Use the landing-page pixel to measure landing page views and later purchase events.
Review actual delivery geography and narrow the audience if the platform is finding cheap clicks from poor-fit areas.

quote.text: So, what that means is if I'm a 72-year-old woman who's not an active member of the LDS church, I'm going to swipe away from that so hard, which is perfect for me
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Post a useful story in communities before adding a link
steps: Choose a relevant community and check its promotion rules and recent high-performing posts.
Tell a true, specific story about the problem and what was built.
Initially leave out the product link; answer questions in the comments and add the link only if allowed.
Use a screenshot or other relevant image in Facebook groups, where the founder says visual posts perform better.

quote.text: as it starts to do well and you see the views climb and you see people are commenting, a answer comments telling people what it is cuz that's usually allowed.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Track ads with a pixel and per-ad UTMs
steps: Install a Meta pixel with view-content, checkout, and purchase events.
Add UTM parameters to the landing-page URL to identify the source ad.
Compare clicks, landing page views, video plays, and purchases instead of relying on click counts alone.
Save a custom Ads Manager column preset containing only the metrics needed for decisions.

quote.text: A UTM parameter is basically adding something like that to a link so you can track where that link came from.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Make setup and checkout low-friction
steps: Allow customers to build an event and generate a link before asking them to pay.
Show prices clearly rather than implying the product is free.
Keep signers account-free and make the form mobile-first.
Check the real click path before claiming a specific number of clicks.

quote.text: A CTA that lies by one click is worse than a boring one.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Choose a simple price and test lifetime access
steps: Start with one annual plan and no free plan.
Consider whether a low one-off lifetime option better fits customers who need the product for one event.
Use actual conversion and retention data before deciding whether to remove a lifetime option.

quote.text: My bet is that people need this for onetime use. We have subscription fatigue, so I'd rather get $17 than $0 from them.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test the complete payment flow before scaling spend
steps: Run the organizer flow from event creation through payment and account setup.
Use test mode while validating, then confirm the live Stripe account is connected before taking real payments.
Verify the generated link and signed-copy workflow after checkout succeeds.
Pause the ad campaign while resolving live checkout errors.

quote.text: So, for now, I'm going to pause my ad. Okay, I did the hard part. I built it. I'm going to pause it. Okay, for now so I don't burn money.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Fix the product from observed user friction
steps: Use screenshots and exact steps to report checkout errors to the coding agent.
Test the product on a real phone and complete a real payment flow.
Add required form fields such as emergency contact and medical information after checking the source form.
Add a working contact form so visitors can report problems.

quote.text: The version of the form that was live a few days ago when I last filmed was not thorough enough. It didn't ask for allergies or emergency contact.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

quote.text: And so, I basically just told Claude, "Don't lie."

warnings.warning: A low annual price can be overwhelmed by paid acquisition costs; the founder says his spend exceeded the first annual subscription.

quote.text: I've clearly lost money. I've spent probably around 100 bucks in ads so far, including the time I spent offline six hours building this app to make $13.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: The app was new and had bugs, so the founder added a contact form and a lifetime refund guarantee to reduce buyer concern.

quote.text: Full transparency. This app is new. 100% lifetime money back guarantee.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Start by solving a problem the founder personally understands, then use that knowledge to choose the first audience and the product requirements.

quote.text: I'm trying to skip the line a little bit. I can probably convert other types of people like, you know, the owner of the gymnastics gym or the trampoline park.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Do not let prompt preparation become a reason to delay building; a workable first prompt can be improved after the product exists.

quote.text: Don't overthink it. Any prompt is better than no prompt. And if coming up with the perfect prompt is enough friction to prevent you from actually doing the thing, then just tell it whatever.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: The final refinement stage can take substantial time, so plan for testing and repeated fixes after the initial build appears complete.

quote.text: The last mile is a real thing. And in logistics, delivery, electricity, whatever it is, the literal last mile is the hardest part.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Test demand while the product is being built, but pause spend when there is no working path for a visitor to become a customer.

quote.text: I'm going to start seeing if I can make ads for this before it's even done because what do I always say? Sell it before you have it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Make the first version simple and remove unnecessary steps from signup and checkout, while being clear about when payment is required.

quote.text: In any business, you want to remove friction to getting the money and add friction to losing the money.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Specific creative can filter out poor-fit viewers and help the ad platform learn from people who engage.

quote.text: So, what that means is if I'm a 72-year-old woman who's not an active member of the LDS church, I'm going to swipe away from that so hard, which is perfect for me
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Measure landing page views and purchases, not just link clicks, because clicking an ad does not mean the visitor reached or bought from the site.

quote.text: Some people click and then they bounce. They need to land on the landing page and Meta knows that they're landing there because I have a pixel there.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Community promotion can work when it starts with an honest, relevant story and respects the rules of the group.

quote.text: the best way to promote on Reddit is to just write a true factual story about what you've done and why you did it and not link to it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Trust signals matter for a new product: show the actual founder and product, state that it is new, and offer a clear way to get in touch.

quote.text: I want people to know that a real human is behind this, that I'm behind this, and that I stand behind these 13 and $17 fees that I'm charging
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: The first customer provides proof that someone will pay, but the founder's own account shows that a sale alone does not prove the economics work.

quote.text: The first dollar for any business is the best dollar in the world. It will never get old. I don't care if it's literally $1, $1,000, doesn't matter.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Use customer and campaign data to adjust the audience instead of assuming the ad platform will automatically find the right buyer.

quote.text: Meta is optimizing for cheap clicks anywhere. You're right to call it. Utah only men 20 to 60 hard age cap kept.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Treat AI as a useful operator but verify its work, provide missing context, and push back when it declines a task or makes the wrong choice.

quote.text: If Claude says it can't do something, it doesn't mean it can't do it. It just probably means it doesn't want to spend credits doing that thing
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: The host demonstrates the build, ad setup, product fixes, campaign measurements, and one external subscription sale. The early operating evidence is first-hand and includes specific process details, but results are very short-term, only one external customer is reported, several metrics are approximate or inconsistent, and unit economics and retention are not established.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris shares a Replit affiliate link and says he would earn $20 from a referral. He also promotes his own channel and business activity.
